content: Drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Women should be advised to use additional non-hormonal contraception during the first seven days of therapy. Tablets should be taken in the order specified on the blister pack calendar at the same time each day. Combined hormonal contraceptives, including drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol, increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) following delivery. This risk decreases rapidly after 21 days but does not return to baseline until 42 days postpartum. According to CDC guidelines, therapy should be initiated 21–42 days postpartum in women without additional VTE risk factors. For postpartum women who do not breastfeed or after a second-trimester abortion, therapy should be delayed for at least four weeks. For those who have had a cesarean section, therapy should be delayed for at least six weeks. Women with additional VTE risk factors postpartum should not use combined hormonal contraceptives. Drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol may be used to treat moderate acne in females aged 14 years or older, but only if oral contraception is chosen as the method of birth control. Ethinyl estradiol increases the levels or effects of fezolinetant by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism, and coadministration is contraindicated. Fezolinetant's AUC and peak plasma concentration are increased when coadministered with weak, moderate, or strong CYP1A2 inhibitors. Ethinyl estradiol coadministration with ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir and dasabuvir is contraindicated due to an unspecified interaction mechanism, which may increase toxicity. ALT elevations greater than five times the upper limit of normal (ULN), and in some cases greater than 20 times ULN, have been observed in clinical trials when ethinyl estradiol was coadministered with these drugs. Ethinyl estradiol-containing medications should be discontinued before initiating ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir and/or dasabuvir and restarted approximately two weeks after completing the hepatitis C combination drug regimen. Coadministration of tranexamic acid and ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated due to increased thrombotic risk from pharmacodynamic synergism. Drospirenone and amiloride both increase serum potassium levels, and their coadministration is contraindicated due to the risk of hyperkalemia. Amobarbital decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism, and alternative drugs should be considered. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced, and non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Ethinyl estradiol decreases the effects of anastrozole by pharmacodynamic antagonism, and concurrent use with estrogens or estrogen-containing products should be avoided. Apalutamide decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by inducing hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Armodafinil decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended as hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Atazanavir may cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, potentially reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Belzutifan decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol and drospirenone by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Coadministration may lead to contraceptive failure or increased breakthrough bleeding. Women of reproductive potential should use effective non-hormonal contraception. Based on animal studies, belzutifan can cause fetal harm. Bosentan decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended as hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Calaspargase pegol may indirectly interact with oral contraceptives, and concomitant use is not recommended. Non-oral contraceptive methods should be used for females of childbearing potential. Brigatinib decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially leading to contraceptive failure. Women should use effective non-hormonal contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. Butabarbital decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Calaspargase pegol may indirectly interact with ethinyl estradiol, and concomitant use is not recommended. Non-oral contraceptive methods should be used. Carbamazepine decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Conivaptan increases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Dexamethasone decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Efavirenz decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Ethinyl estradiol decreases the effects of elagolix by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended during treatment and for one week after discontinuation. Elvitegravir decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by an unknown mechanism. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. Enasidenib increases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by affecting OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or BCRP substrates. Coadministration should be avoided, and substrate dosage should be adjusted if unavoidable.
